claims.text: The enhanced corrosion resistance of steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is primarily caused by a homogenized microstructure.
Elemental segregation at grain boundaries is detrimental to corrosion resistance.
Minimizing grain-boundary segregation facilitates formation of a uniform passivating oxide film.
The corrosion-protective passive film is rich in chromium.
A uniform chromium-rich passive film is self-healing and blocks corrosive species.
Commercial stainless steels in as-received or conventionally processed states exhibit variable grain-boundary elemental segregation.
Controlled annealing can reduce grain-boundary segregation in the steels under study.
Controlled annealing can promote a homogeneous distribution of passivating elements.
Exposure to 0.5 M sulfuric acid can be used to represent chemical-processing corrosion conditions.
Elevated-temperature high-purity water can be used to represent nuclear-power aqueous conditions.
Uniform availability of chromium across the microstructure promotes rapid formation of a defect-free passive oxide.
The passive oxide limits ion transport.
Limiting ion transport through the passive oxide suppresses localized corrosion initiation.
Annealed samples with minimized segregation will have a wider passivation-potential range than untreated samples.
Annealed samples with minimized segregation will have lower corrosion current densities than untreated samples.
Annealed samples with minimized segregation will develop a more uniform, adherent, and chemically stable oxide film than untreated samples.
The proposed mechanism should operate under laboratory environments representative of chemical-processing plants and nuclear-reactor aqueous service.
Severe mechanical wear or conditions far outside the specified chemical and aqueous environments may reduce the benefit of microstructural homogenization.
